General obligation bonds. Refers to bonds issued by a state or local government that are payable from either an issuer’s general fund or specific taxes (usually property tax). The precise source and priority of payment for general obligation bonds may vary among issuers depending on applicable state and local laws.
Revenue bonds. Instead of taxes, these bonds are backed by revenues from a specific project or source, such as highway tolls or lease fees.
answer: General obligation (GO) bonds and revenue bonds differ in what backs their payments. GO bonds issued by state or local governments are payable from the issuer’s general fund or specific taxes, often property taxes; the exact payment source and priority can vary by issuer and applicable law. Revenue bonds are backed instead by income from a particular project or source, such as highway tolls or lease fees. Some revenue bonds are non-recourse, meaning bondholders may have no claim on the underlying revenue source if that revenue dries up.
